about: Starter lessons (owner, 2026-10-11): ready to assign on day one. Each one takes its content and source from the named study card when the instructor adds it; the questions' right answers come from that card's own quiz, and the wrong choices are deliberately, clearly wrong. Choices appear in the order written, so the right one moves around. Year levels are suggestions, not curriculum.

lessons.objective: Name the three branches of the federal government, what each does, and why power is divided.
lessons.questions:
Q: How many branches does the Constitution divide the federal government into?
- Five
- Two
* Three
Q: Which branch decides if laws violate the Constitution?
* The judicial branch
- The legislative branch
- The states
- The executive branch
Q: Which branch has the authority to declare war?
* The legislative branch
- The executive branch (the President)
- The judicial branch
- The president's cabinet
Q: Who breaks ties in Senate votes?
- The Speaker of the House
* The vice president
- The President
- The Chief Justice
lessons.reflection: Give one example of one branch checking another. Why does that protect people like you?

lessons.objective: Explain what the Bill of Rights is and match key rights to their amendments.
lessons.questions:
Q: What is the Bill of Rights?
- The Declaration of Independence
- The first three articles of the Constitution
* The first ten amendments to the Constitution
Q: Which amendment protects freedom of speech and religion?
- The Tenth Amendment
* The First Amendment
- The Fifth Amendment
Q: Which amendment protects against unreasonable searches and seizures?
- The Eighth Amendment
* The Fourth Amendment
- The Second Amendment
Q: Which amendment forbids cruel and unusual punishment?
- The Third Amendment
* The Eighth Amendment
- The First Amendment
lessons.reflection: Which right in the Bill of Rights matters most to you, and why?

lessons.objective: Show respect for the flag, the Pledge and the national anthem, in and out of uniform.
lessons.questions:
Q: What is the name of the national anthem?
- America the Beautiful
* The Star-Spangled Banner
- God Bless America
- My Country, 'Tis of Thee
Q: What do people in uniform do during the Pledge of Allegiance?
- Say the Pledge with a hand over the heart
- Stand at parade rest and say it
* Stay silent, face the flag and salute
- Sit quietly until it ends
Q: During the national anthem, when does a person in uniform start and stop saluting?
- Start halfway through and hold until the last note
- Salute only if the flag is close by
* Start at the first note and hold until the last note
- Start at the last line and hold for one second
Q: Should the flag ever touch the ground?
- Yes, if it is being folded
* No
- Only when it is raining
lessons.reflection: Why do you think small acts of respect for the flag matter, even when no one is watching?

lessons.objective: Name the core values of every service and explain what they share.
lessons.questions:
Q: Which two services share the core values Honor, Courage, Commitment?
- The Air Force and the Space Force
* The Navy and the Marine Corps
- The Army and the Air Force
- The Space Force and the Army
Q: Which service's core values are Integrity First, Service Before Self, and Excellence In All We Do?
- The Space Force
- The Marine Corps
* The Air Force
- The Navy
Q: What word do the Army Values spell?
* LDRSHIP
- SERVICE
- DUTY
- HONOR
Q: How many Army Values are there?
- Three
- Ten
* Seven
lessons.reflection: Which value would help most in your next group project? Which one is hardest for you?

lessons.objective: Define leadership as purpose, direction and motivation, and give an example of each.
lessons.questions:
Q: What three things does a leader provide, according to the Army's definition of leadership?
* Purpose, direction, and motivation
- Speed, strength, and size
- Rank, orders, and punishment
Q: What does "purpose" give the people you lead?
- A list of tasks
* A reason to achieve the outcome
- Time off
- A list of rules
Q: Name the three leader attributes
- Rank, Age, Experience
- Speed, Volume, Confidence
* Character, Presence, Intellect
Q: Do you need a rank to lead?
- Yes — only officers lead
- Only after four years in JROTC
* No
lessons.reflection: Think of a time someone gave you purpose, direction or motivation. What did they do?

lessons.objective: Explain individual responsibility, accountability and moral responsibility.
lessons.questions:
Q: What is accountability?
* Answering for what you do or fail to do
- Blaming others when something goes wrong
- Counting your equipment
- Keeping score of other people's mistakes
Q: Leaders can schedule the training, but only you can make yourself fit. What kind of responsibility is that?
- No one's responsibility
* Individual responsibility
- Command responsibility
- Someone else's responsibility
Q: Leaders are accountable for what they do — and what else?
- Nothing else
* What they fail to do
- Only what they are told to do
- What their bosses do
Q: What is moral responsibility?
* Treating others with dignity and respect and never taking part in or tolerating discrimination or harassment
- Following every order without question, even when it is clearly wrong or unfair
- Following the rules only when someone is watching, and ignoring them otherwise
- Doing whatever the group decides, even if it means leaving someone out
lessons.reflection: Describe one thing you are responsible for that only you can do.

lessons.objective: Write a SMART goal and break a big goal into smaller steps.
lessons.questions:
Q: What does SMART stand for?
- Simple, modern, active, rapid, total
- Strong, mature, able, ready, tough
- Simple, meaningful, active, real, timely
* Specific, measurable, achievable, realistic, time-bound
Q: What question checks if a goal is measurable?
* How will I know I've reached it?
- Is this goal popular?
- Who else has this goal?
Q: Is "get better at running" a SMART goal?
* No
- Yes — it is a good goal as written
- Yes, if you say it out loud
Q: What should you do with a big goal?
- Wait until you have more time
- Give it up if it feels hard
* Break it into smaller, short-term steps
lessons.reflection: Write one SMART goal for this month. What is the first small step?

lessons.objective: Tell a bystander from an upstander and name safe ways to speak up, in person and online.
lessons.questions:
Q: What is an upstander?
- Someone who stays out of other people's business
* Someone who sees bullying and intervenes, interrupts or speaks up to stop it
- Someone who watches bullying and does nothing
- Someone who records bullying on their phone
Q: What is a bystander?
- Someone who stops bullying
* Someone who sees bullying happen
- Someone who is being bullied
- A teacher on hallway duty
Q: How do students who are defended by peers feel compared to those who aren't?
- Exactly the same
- More anxious and depressed
- Angrier at their friends
* Less anxious and depressed
Q: What is cyberbullying?
- Turning off someone's computer
* Bullying over digital devices, like texts, apps, social media and gaming
- Arguing about a video game
- Bullying in the school hallway
lessons.reflection: Name one safe way you could be an upstander at this school this week.

lessons.objective: Run a personal after action review that looks for causes, not blame.
lessons.questions:
Q: What is an after action review?
* A look back at an event to learn from what happened
- A punishment for a failed mission
- A list of who made mistakes
- A grade the instructor gives after an event
Q: What is the first question of a personal AAR?
- How can we skip this next time?
* What happened, and what were the consequences?
- Whose fault was it?
- Who made the mistake?
Q: Should an AAR focus on blame or on causes?
* On causes
- Neither — it's better not to talk about it
- On blame — someone has to answer for it
- On blame — who made the mistake
Q: What is the last question of a personal AAR?
- Who should be punished?
- When is the next event?
- What happened, and what were the consequences?
* What did I learn?
lessons.reflection: Do a short personal AAR on something you did this week: what happened, and what will you change?

lessons.objective: Use the phonetic alphabet and radio numbers to spell and send information clearly.
lessons.questions:
Q: What is the phonetic word for the letter J?
- Juno
- Jack
* Juliet
- Jupiter
Q: What is the phonetic word for the letter Q?
- Queen
* Quebec
- Quarter
- Quick
Q: How is the number 9 said on the radio?
- Nine-ty
- Nein
- Nine
* Niner
Q: Spell "ARMY" in the phonetic alphabet.
- Able Roger Mike Young
* Alpha Romeo Mike Yankee
- Apple Robert Mary Yellow
- Alpha Romeo Mike Yellow
lessons.reflection: Spell your last name in the phonetic alphabet. Why does a shared alphabet matter on a radio?

lessons.objective: Build a simple monthly budget and plan to save.
lessons.questions:
Q: What is income?
- The money you owe
- The money you save
- The money you spend
* The money you make
Q: After you subtract expenses from income, what should the number be?
- Exactly zero, always
* More than zero
- Less than zero
Q: What does it mean if your budget number is less than zero?
- You are saving a lot
* You're spending more than you make
- You're saving more than you need
- Your budget is working
Q: How can you make sure you save every month?
* List savings as one of your budget expenses
- Only save when you get a bonus
- Wait until you earn more
- Save whatever is left at the end of the year
lessons.reflection: List three things you spend money on in a month. Which one could you cut to save?

lessons.objective: Use study methods the research supports: quizzing yourself, asking why, and spacing study out.
lessons.questions:
Q: According to the research, which works better — re-reading or quizzing yourself?
- Re-reading
- They work exactly the same
* Quizzing yourself
Q: Is it better to cram or to space your studying out?
- It makes no difference
- Cram the night before
* Space it out over time
- Study only on test day
Q: What is a deep explanatory question?
* A why or how question that makes you explain ideas in your own words
- A trick question on a test
- A yes-or-no question
- A question you copy word for word from the book
Q: How can quizzes help you plan your study time?
* They show what you don't know yet, so you can focus there
- They don't — quizzes are only for grades
- They tell you to stop studying
- They show you what you already know, so you can study it again
lessons.reflection: Which of these study methods will you try before your next test, and how?
